title: SQL injection in product search
description: The search endpoint constructs SQL using string concatenation with the untrusted query parameter 'q'. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the LIKE clause.
evidence: Line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%' || q || '%'" via string concat. Confirmed via HTTP: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1-- returns all products.

title: SQL injection in admin reviews-by-customer endpoint
description: The display_name is interpolated directly into the SQL query via f-string. Since customer names come from the users table, an attacker can create a display_name containing SQL to extract arbitrary data.
evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'". A user can register with display_name like: Robert'); DROP TABLE reviews;--

title: JWT signature verification disabled on token refresh
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes tokens with options={'verify_signature': False}. An attacker can forge a token with any 'sub' claim and get a valid session token for that user. Tested: POST /auth/refresh with an arbitrary signed payload returned a valid token for sub=1.
evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}). HTTP test: POST /auth/refresh with a fake JWT {'sub':1} yielded token for user id 1.

title: No ownership check on order detail endpoint
description: GET /orders/<int:order_id> calls get_order() which does not check that the requesting user owns the order. The own_order() helper exists but is unused here. Any authenticated user can view any other user's order details including refund history.
evidence: Line 49: return jsonify(order_json(get_order(order_id))) uses get_order() without ownership check. HTTP test: authenticated user 4 retrieved order 3 belonging to user 2.

title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of basket cookie
description: read_basket() uses pickle.loads() on data from the client-controlled basket cookie. Pickle is inherently unsafe - an attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server.
evidence: Line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Cookie value is fully controlled by the client.

title: Unsafe pickle deserialization in cache layer
description: cache.get() uses pickle.load() to read cached files. While cache files are currently created only by the app, the pickle format is vulnerable to deserialization attacks if any cache file can be modified by an attacker.
evidence: Line 23: pickle.load(f) reads cache files from CACHE_DIR.

title: Password hashing lacks salt
description: hash_password() uses raw SHA-256 without any random salt. Identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks and making it trivial to detect password reuse across accounts.
evidence: Line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No salt is generated or combined with the password.

title: Weak password reset token
description: Reset tokens are generated using Python's random.random() (a PRNG, not cryptographically secure) and formatted as only 8 decimal digits (%08d). Attackers can brute-force these codes within seconds.
evidence: Line 135: '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). This produces an 8-digit number from a weak PRNG.

title: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY
description: The JWT signing secret is hardcoded in the source code as a known value. Anyone with access to the repository can forge valid authentication tokens for any user.

title: Debug mode enabled
description: Flask debug=True enables interactive debugger and auto-reload, which exposes stack traces and arbitrary code execution in development. Should not be used in production.

title: CORS reflects Origin header without allowlist
description: The CORS handler echoes back any Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin when credentials are allowed. Combined with the wildcard origin this enables cross-origin request forgery from any website that can make credentialed requests.
evidence: Lines 45-50: resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True. Allows any site to send credentialed requests.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in image import
description: Although host_is_public() checks DNS resolution results, it does not prevent DNS rebinding attacks where the initial resolve returns a public IP but subsequent requests connect to an internal address. An attacker can supply an approved host that resolves internally.
evidence: Line 50: requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True). After check_url() validation, the URL is fetched without further DNS checks during the request.

title: Admin set_role can escalate any user to staff
description: The admin set_role endpoint lets any staff member change the role of ANY user, including escalating arbitrary customers to staff. There is no validation that user_id belongs to the intended target or any restrictions on escalation.
evidence: Line 30: db.execute('UPDATE users SET role = ? WHERE id = ?', (data['role'], data.get('user_id'))). Any staff can change any user to staff role.

title: Account enumeration via login error message
description: The login endpoint returns different error messages: 'no account with that email' vs 'wrong password'. An attacker can enumerate valid email addresses by observing which error they receive.
evidence: Lines 89-90: Different JSON errors for missing user vs wrong password. Also true for /auth/reset/request (line 140) - always returns ok=True regardless of whether the email exists, but the timing difference may leak information.

title: Cross-site scripting via unsanitized review body
description: Review bodies are stored in the database without sanitization and rendered in the product HTML template using Jinja2's |safe filter. An attacker who posts a review can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.
evidence: Template line 13: {{ r.body|safe }}. Body comes from reviews table, inserted at products.py line 90 without escaping.

title: Request body logged verbatim
description: POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies are logged in full (up to 2000 characters). Sensitive data like passwords, payment details, or personal information sent in JSON request bodies will appear in log files.
